newsitem.title: GERMANY: German PPI rise sparks no inflation fears.
newsitem.headline: German PPI rise sparks no inflation fears.

text.p: Pan-German producer prices climbed 0.2 percent in October, but were still 0.3 percent below the level of October 1995, the economics ministry said on Friday.
Import prices, meanwhile, were up 0.6 percent from the previous month and 1.6 percent year-on-year. Export prices were up 0.2 percent on a monthly basis, but remained unchanged year-on-year.

Economists said the data gave them no reason to expect a rise in inflation or a change in interest rates, as the producer and import price increases were linked to an increase in oil prices, and have not filtered on to consumer prices.

"This is not at all a case of inflation," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt. "The increase in prices is related to some increases in crude oil and heating oil prices."
Oil prices have edged up in recent weeks as cold weather crept across North America, Europe, North Asia and Japan.

Grebe also noted that the producer price rise was matched at the same time by indications of a dip in consumer prices. The state statistics office in Baden-Wurttemberg on Friday said its October consumer prices were down 0.1 percent over the previous month and were up 1.3 percent year-over-year.
The states of Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Bavaria plan to publish their price data on Monday.
"If you look at all areas of the economy, prices are still on a downward trend," Grebe said.

"It's nothing for the Bundesbank to worry about," added Hermann Remsperger, BHF Bank chief economist in Frankfurt. "Prices are very favourable. Even if there is a slight increase in raw material prices, they are balanced off by restructuring in the economy and improvements in productivity."
The stable price situation also bodes well for stable interest rates, the economists said.
"We think the Bundesbank is going to stay on an unchanging course on interest rates," said Dresdner Bank economist Rolf Schneider in Frankfurt.

Grebe also discounted any combined effect from the producer price rise and a recent slight increase in the key M3 money supply, which he attributed to this week's historic float of Deutsche Telekom AG.
"Telekom had a temporary effect," he said. "M3 may be up a bit in November but I think it will go down again in December."
Higher oil prices combined with a dip in the mark in October, when the dollar spiked to 1.54 DM, to push up import prices, the economists said.
"In the past we have said import prices would fluctuate as the mark fluctuates," Remsperger said. "We don't see that changing much in the next few months."
